items.prompt: A page creates 1,000 `Cart` instances. How many copies of the `addItem` function exist, and why?
items.answer: One: class methods live on Cart.prototype and every instance reaches them through the prototype chain
distractors: 1,000: the class body re-creates every method inside each `new Cart()` call
1,000 until the first call, after which the engine merges them into a single shared copy
None until called: methods are compiled lazily per instance on first use
items.explanation: The lesson: methods like addItem and getTotal are shared through the class prototype rather than recreated on every instance; classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes. (Only `this.items` is per instance.)

items.prompt: `parseUser('{"age": 31}')` is called. The JSON is valid. What does the caller get back?
items.answer: null: the missing-name check throws inside the try, so the same catch that handles bad JSON logs it and returns null
distractors: The object { age: 31 }, because the catch only handles JSON.parse syntax errors
An Error thrown to the caller, since a throw written by hand is not caught by its own try
undefined, because the function stops at the throw without reaching any return
items.explanation: Both failure modes the lesson names (invalid JSON, missing required data) end in the one catch block.

items.prompt: The Lab 03C `safeParse(json, fallback)` is used for a settings file. What does it give up compared with the lesson's `parseUser`?
items.answer: Any trace of the failure: it neither logs nor validates, so a corrupt file and a file that genuinely holds the fallback value look identical
distractors: Nothing: an optional catch binding still logs the error automatically
It rethrows parse errors to the caller, so it is less safe than parseUser
It cannot parse arrays, because the fallback parameter defaults to null
items.explanation: `catch { return fallback; }` swallows the error entirely; parseUser at least logs `error.message` and checks required data.

items.prompt: With the reference `BankAccount`, a fresh account receives `deposit(20)` then `withdraw(50)`. What is `getBalance()`, and what does that reveal about the solution?
items.answer: -30: withdraw subtracts unconditionally, so the class enforces no business rule against overdrawing (or negative amounts)
distractors: 20: withdraw ignores amounts larger than the balance
0: the balance is clamped at zero by the subtraction assignment
It throws a RangeError when the balance would go below zero
items.explanation: The solution only shows the class shape; `this.balance -= amount` has no guard. A real account would validate before mutating.

items.prompt: Why is `import { double } from "./math.js"` better than defining `double` as a global that app.js just uses?
items.answer: The dependency is named at the top of app.js, and anything math.js does not export stays private to that module instead of leaking into shared global scope
distractors: Imported functions run faster because modules are compiled ahead of time
import copies the function, so app.js cannot be affected by later changes to math.js
Globals cannot be called across files at all, so the import is the only option
items.explanation: Modules reduce hidden global state and make reuse explicit (the lesson's line under the example).

items.prompt: Why does `loadPosts` test `response.ok` itself instead of trusting its catch block to see failed requests?
items.answer: fetch only rejects on network-level failures; a 404 or 500 still resolves, so without the explicit throw the error path would never run
distractors: The check makes fetch retry the request once before the catch runs
await throws for 4xx statuses but not for 5xx, so the check covers server errors only
response.json() would block the event loop on an error status unless ok is checked first
items.explanation: The lesson calls this a common beginner mistake: assuming fetch throws on every failed HTTP status.

items.prompt: A button handler runs `loadPosts(); console.log("after");` without awaiting. When does "after" print relative to the posts appearing?
items.answer: Before them: await suspends only loadPosts, so the handler continues as soon as loadPosts hits its first await
distractors: After the posts render, because await inside loadPosts blocks the whole program
Never, since an un-awaited async call cancels the rest of the handler
Exactly one second later, because pending fetches delay synchronous logs
items.explanation: The lesson: `await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program.

items.prompt: In the Lab 05 solutions, the users endpoint returns 503. What does the #status element finally say?
items.answer: "Error: Status: 503": loadUsers throws, its promise rejects, and the awaited call inside showUsers' try lands in the catch
distractors: "Loaded users.", because loadUsers has no try/catch of its own and so cannot fail
"Loading..." forever, because a rejection inside another async function is not visible to the caller
Nothing at all, because the list is emptied before the status is updated
items.explanation: An error thrown in an async function becomes a rejection; `await loadUsers()` re-throws it in showUsers, whose catch writes the message.

items.prompt: Why does `wait(ms)` build `new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms))` instead of just returning `setTimeout(...)`?
items.answer: setTimeout returns a timer id, not something awaitable; handing resolve to the timer gives callers a promise that settles when the delay ends
distractors: setTimeout already returns a promise, but wrapping it adds error handling
The wrapper makes the delay run on a separate thread so it cannot block rendering
Without the wrapper the timer would fire immediately because ms is ignored
items.explanation: The lesson presents it as the promise version of a delay; then `.then` / `await` can wait on it.

items.prompt: `app.use(express.json())` is deleted. A client POSTs `{"title":"Ship it"}` with a JSON content type. Does a task get created?
items.answer: No: nothing parses the body, so req.body is not populated and the handler cannot read the title
distractors: Yes: Express parses JSON bodies by default and the middleware only adds validation
Yes, but the title is stored as the raw JSON string
No, because express.json() is what registers the POST route
items.explanation: The lesson: express.json() parses JSON request bodies so req.body is usable.

items.prompt: In `POST /tasks`, the `return` before `res.status(400)` is removed. A request arrives with title "   ". What goes wrong?
items.answer: The handler keeps going after the 400: it stores a task with an empty title and tries to send a second response
distractors: Nothing: sending a response automatically ends the route handler
The request hangs, because res.status without return never sends anything
Express rejects the blank title itself before the handler runs
items.explanation: The lesson's order is parse, validate, apply logic, store, respond; `return` is what stops invalid input from reaching the store.

items.prompt: The tasks API is scaled to two instances behind a load balancer, still using `const tasks = []`. A user creates a task, then lists tasks. What can happen?
items.answer: The list request may reach the other instance, whose separate array never saw the task
distractors: Both instances share the array, because module-level variables are global to the host
The second request blocks until the first instance replicates its array
The task appears twice, once from each instance's copy
items.explanation: The lesson lists the limits of an in-memory array: lost on restart, does not scale across multiple instances.

items.prompt: What makes the `isValidEmail` tests short and reliable, according to the lesson?
items.answer: The function has one job and no hidden external state, so a given input always produces the same checkable output
distractors: Node's built-in runner retries failing assertions until they pass
strict assert ignores type differences between true and "true"
The tests mock the email server, so no network is involved
items.explanation: Pure functions are listed first among the easiest high-value test targets.

items.prompt: You changed one thing and the error message went away. Per the lesson's workflow, what must you still do before calling the bug fixed?
items.answer: Re-run the original reproduction path, since the symptom vanishing is not proof the reported behavior is now correct
distractors: Revert the change and try a different one to confirm it was not luck
Add a comment explaining the fix, which replaces re-testing
Change the surrounding layers too, so the same class of bug cannot recur
items.explanation: Steps 5 and 6: fix one thing at a time, then re-test the original reproduction path.

items.front: The tasks API assigns `id: Date.now()`. Two POSTs land within the same millisecond. What breaks later?
items.back: Both tasks get the same id, so a DELETE or PATCH by id (Labs 07A/07B) hits the wrong task or both. Use a counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or a database key.

items.front: Both lesson tests pass, yet `isValidEmail("@.")` returns what — and what does that say about the two tests?
items.back: true: it only checks that "@" and "." appear somewhere. Two happy/sad examples did not pin down the rule; add edge cases (missing local part, dot before @).

items.front:
`loadPosts` renders with `list.innerHTML = posts.map(post => `
  • ${post.title}
    • `)`. A post title contains ``. What happens?
items.back: The markup is parsed and the handler runs (XSS). Build elements and set textContent for API data, or escape it, instead of interpolating into innerHTML.

items.front: A caller of `parseUser` gets null. Can it tell whether the input was broken JSON or a user without a name?
items.back: No: both failures go through one catch and return null; only the console log differs. Return a result with a reason, or throw distinct errors, when callers must react differently.
